A_target.statement:
Let $\map P \phi$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|property]] of [[Definition:Well-Formed Formula|formulas]] of [[Definition:First-Order Logic|first-order logic]].
Suppose $\map P \phi$ holds for [[Definition:Atomic Formula|atomic formulas]], and is preserved by $\neg$, $\land$ and $\exists$.
Then $\map P \phi$ holds for all formulas $\phi$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\map P n$ be a [[Definition:Propositional Function|propositional function]] on $\N$.
If $\map P 0$ holds and $\map P n \implies \map P {n + 1}$, then $\map P n$ holds for all $n \in \N$.

substitutions.the induction hypothesis at n: the hypothesis at all immediate subformulas

derived.the well-ordering of the naturals: the well-foundedness of the subformula relation

object_map.reformulation: The induction must be reindexed by a complexity measure before the naturals-based skeleton applies, since formulas are not themselves numbers.

validity_conditions: formulas must be uniquely readable, so each formula has a well-defined set of immediate subformulas
the subformula relation must be well founded, which follows from finiteness of formulas
the step case must cover every formation rule, or the induction has a gap
proof_plan: Assign to each formula $\phi$ its [[Definition:Complexity of Formula|complexity]] $\map c \phi$, the number of connectives and quantifiers in $\phi$.

Immediate subformulas have strictly smaller complexity:
:$\map c \psi < \map c {\neg \psi}, \map c {\psi \land \chi}, \map c {\exists x \, \psi}$
Apply the [[Second Principle of Mathematical Induction|strong form of induction]] on $\map c \phi \in \N$.

Atomic formulas have complexity $0$, giving the base case.
Each formation rule gives a step case, using the hypothesis for the immediate subformulas.
